case_study_insert.main_stem: Zenith Smart Payments (ZEN) is a private limited company in the financial technology sector, providing contactless payment terminals and online checkout software to retailers across Singapore and Malaysia. Founded in 2012 by Daniel Ong, it employs a workforce of 52 and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. ZEN plans to invest $840,000 in a contactless payment platform upgrade with integrated e-commerce checkout and fraud screening, financed by a $500,000 five-year bank loan and $340,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $264,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.00, and currently produces 84,000 units a year. ZEN faces two problems: its checkout software has a 6.2% transaction failure rate, and a shortage of cybersecurity skills is slowing the upgrade.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: ZEN processed 18,600 checkout transactions last quarter, of which 6.2% failed at payment authorisation, down from 9.4% a year earlier. Support tickets averaged 34 a day and 14 of 40 merchant clients now require a written fraud-control plan before renewal. Average integration time for a new merchant is 2.1 days. Platform uptime was 99.4%. Market research of 450 merchants found that 68% would pay up to $0.60 more for fraud-protected checkout, and 57% check security certification before switching supplier. A skills audit shows 16 of 52 staff lack advanced cybersecurity training; an external certification course costs $780 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Zenith Smart Payments for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.80 to $13.62 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across the technology sector. (3) Cloud hosting and data-centre input costs have risen 11.8% year-on-year, while digital-payment transaction volumes grew 5.2% and consumer spending on online retail rose 3.9%.

questions.question_text: ZEN plans to fund part of its $840,000 platform upgrade with a $500,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for ZEN of using the $340,000 retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge and no fixed repayment schedule, which protects ZEN's cash flow while it already covers fixed costs of $264,000 a year and services a $500,000 bank loan. Each dollar of interest avoided can be spent on reducing the 6.2% checkout failure rate, for example by expanding the fraud-screening team, without raising the $13.00 selling price or squeezing the $7.50 contribution per unit. With the base rate due to climb to 5.25% (Appendix 3), a variable-rate loan would grow more expensive, so using the $340,000 already earned removes that exposure entirely.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership and control with founder Daniel Ong and the existing shareholders, and it avoids the collateral and covenants a $500,000 loan would impose on the $840,000 platform. No lender could repossess the upgraded checkout system if merchant demand grows more slowly than expected, which matters because 14 of 40 merchant clients now demand a fraud-control plan before renewal. It is also faster than renegotiating debt, letting ZEN respond to the 57% of surveyed merchants who check security certification before switching supplier.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ZEN's costs, financing and merchant relationships.

questions.question_text: ZEN is launching fraud-protected checkout. Consider advertising in a payments trade journal, sponsoring a fintech conference, or running a LinkedIn influencer campaign aimed at merchants. Which should ZEN choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Payments trade journal advertising: A technical advert in a payments trade title reaches acquiring banks, fintech partners and merchant technology managers directly, and it can carry the evidence that 14 of 40 merchant clients now require, such as the fall in checkout failures from 9.4% to 6.2%. Readership is small, but almost every reader influences a purchase decision, and the message can explain fraud screening in detail. Its weakness is that it cannot reach the 450 merchants in ZEN's own survey who are not trade readers, and print lead times are long while the $840,000 upgrade is already under way.

Fintech conference sponsorship: A stand at a regional fintech conference puts ZEN in front of hundreds of merchants and payment partners in two days, with live demonstrations and face-to-face trust building. That suits a technical product and the 57% of merchants who check security certification. However, sponsorship and travel are expensive, the audience is temporary, and enquiries are hard to convert without a follow-up team, which is scarce while 16 of 52 staff lack advanced cybersecurity training.

LinkedIn influencer campaign: Payments and e-commerce influencers can demonstrate fraud-protected checkout with real transaction data to a targeted audience of merchants at low cost per contact, and every click is measurable. The message can speak directly to the 68% of 450 surveyed merchants who would pay $0.60 more for protection. Credibility depends on the influencer and business-audience reach is narrower than mass media, but the audience is exactly ZEN's buyer.

Recommendation: ZEN should choose the LinkedIn influencer campaign. It targets the merchants identified in its own research, costs far less than conference sponsorship, and scales beyond the narrow readership of a trade journal. The trade journal is rejected as too slow and too narrow to launch an $840,000 platform, and conference sponsorship is rejected as a short, expensive event that cannot be sustained while 16 of 52 staff still need cybersecurity training. ZEN should repost the strongest influencer content in its trade advertising afterwards.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to ZEN's merchant market.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some contextual evidence and emerging judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options using ZEN's survey data, skills shortage and expansion budget, with a justified recommendation that explains why the other two are rejected.

questions.question_text: ZEN's checkout failure rate has reached 6.2% and it faces a cybersecurity skills shortage. Explain two benefits for ZEN of democratic leadership and a flat structure in addressing these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 52 employees a genuine say in how the new fraud-screening routines are introduced, which supports their social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Engineers who help set the test schedule for the $840,000 platform are more likely to report faults early, so the 6.2% checkout failure rate can be pushed down further, protecting the 18,600 transactions processed each quarter and reducing the 34 support tickets a day that staff currently handle.

Point 2: A flat organisational structure shortens the chain of command, so a security flaw or a merchant complaint can reach the engineers who can fix it within hours rather than passing through several management layers. That matters when 14 of 40 merchant clients require a written fraud-control plan before renewal and platform uptime is 99.4%. Combined with democratic leadership, the structure encourages the staff with cybersecurity skills to mentor the 16 of 52 who lack advanced training, easing the skills shortage without paying the full $780 per employee course fee, while keeping output of 84,000 units on track.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to ZEN's checkout failures, skills gap and merchant demands.

questions.question_text: ZEN must train 16 staff in advanced cybersecurity. Consider an in-house e-learning platform or an external certification course costing $780 per employee. Which should ZEN choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
In-house e-learning platform: An e-learning platform can be rolled out to all 16 affected staff at once for far less than the $780 per employee external course, and modules can be built around ZEN's own checkout software and the fraud-screening rules behind the 6.2% failure rate. Staff learn at their own pace between handling the 34 support tickets a day, so no one is taken away from merchant support. The drawbacks are weaker practical testing, less interaction with an expert trainer, and a risk that staff finish modules without being able to respond to a real security incident.

External certification course: The $780 per employee course gives a recognised qualification and expert instruction for the 16 staff, which directly answers the 14 of 40 merchants who demand a fraud-control plan and the 57% who check security certification. It briefly removes staff from normal duties and costs $12,480 for the group (16 × $780), a meaningful sum while ZEN is funding an $840,000 upgrade and servicing a $500,000 loan.

Decision: ZEN should choose the external certification course for the 16 staff, supported by short in-house e-learning refreshers. A recognised certificate carries weight with merchants in a way that internal modules do not, and $12,480 is modest beside the $840,000 platform; the 6.2% checkout failure rate makes credible security evidence urgent. The e-learning platform is rejected as the main route because it cannot supply the certification that 57% of surveyed merchants look for, though it remains useful for ongoing updates once the team is qualified.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to ZEN's skills gap.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in ZEN's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensively evaluates both methods against cost, disruption and merchant credibility, with a clear decision and explicit reasons for rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ZEN's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data to plan the platform upgrade.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $264,000 ÷ ($13.00 − $5.50) = $264,000 ÷ $7.50 = 35,200 units. Answer: break-even output is 35,200 units a year.
Formula: Margin of safety = Current output − Break-even output. Substitution: 84,000 − 35,200 = 48,800 units. Answer: margin of safety is 48,800 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ZEN's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing break-even output of 35,200 units with actual output of 84,000 units gives ZEN a margin of safety of 48,800 units, so even a sharp rise in the 6.2% checkout failure rate would still leave the platform covering its $264,000 fixed costs.
2. Contribution per unit of $7.50 lets managers test the $0.60 premium that 68% of surveyed merchants would accept: raising price to $13.60 lifts contribution to $8.10 and cuts break-even to about 32,600 units, showing whether a price rise is better than chasing volume.
3. The same $7.50 figure helps judge whether the $500,000 bank loan can be serviced from the 48,800-unit margin of safety before further capital is committed, especially with the base rate due to reach 5.25%.
4. Average total cost of $8.64 a unit ($264,000 ÷ 84,000 = $3.14, plus $5.50) gives a benchmark for the $840,000 upgrade: if the new platform lifts output or cuts failures without raising variable cost, unit cost falls and contribution widens.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 35,200 units | (ii) Margin of safety = 48,800 units | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: safety margin of 48,800 units against the 6.2% failure rate; testing the $0.60 premium on $7.50 contribution; loan servicing on the $500,000 borrowing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $8.64 for the $840,000 platform.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ZEN's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has ZEN's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 19.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $1,280,000 ÷ revenue $3,200,000 × 100 = 40.0; 2025 $1,710,000 ÷ $3,800,000 × 100 = 45.0, with cost of sales rising only from $1,920,000 to $2,090,000. Operating profit $384,000 ÷ revenue $3,200,000 × 100 = 12.0 in 2024 and $570,000 ÷ $3,800,000 × 100 = 15.0 in 2025. Returns on capital: $384,000 ÷ $2,400,000 × 100 = 16.0 in 2024 and $570,000 ÷ $3,000,000 × 100 = 19.0 in 2025. Interest payable rose from $42,000 to $56,000 after the $500,000 borrowing, yet operating profit still grew faster.

Evaluation: Every measure moved favourably. The gross margin widened from 40.0% to 45.0%, showing that ZEN kept direct costs under control while revenue grew $600,000, helped by the 5.2% rise in digital-payment volumes and the shift towards fraud-protected checkout. The operating margin improved from 12.0% to 15.0%, so more of each revenue dollar survives the $264,000 fixed costs even after interest rose by $14,000. Returns on capital climbed from 16.0% to 19.0% despite capital employed increasing by $600,000, evidence that the new platform is already earning its keep. The gains look genuine because revenue and gross profit both grew, not because prices were cut. The caution is that 6.2% of checkouts still fail, 16 of 52 staff lack cybersecurity training, and cloud costs are rising 11.8%; any of these could erase the improvement if the $840,000 upgrade is badly managed.

Conclusion: ZEN's financial performance has improved. All three measures rose together on the back of higher revenue, and the business has headroom to service the $500,000 loan. ZEN should protect the gain by using part of the retained profit to close the cybersecurity skills gap before the next renewal cycle.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates all three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest, and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ZEN of introducing fraud-protected checkout with AI screening.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Fraud-protected checkout directly answers the 68% of 450 surveyed merchants who would pay up to $0.60 more for it, so ZEN can protect its $7.50 contribution per unit and even improve it while covering the $264,000 fixed costs. It also addresses the 14 of 40 merchant clients who require a written fraud-control plan before renewal, and the 57% who check security certification, helping ZEN keep listings for its $13.00 software and justify the $840,000 platform.

Disadvantage: AI screening adds to the $5.50 variable cost per unit through extra cloud hosting, whose input costs have already risen 11.8%, so the $0.60 premium must be accepted widely or contribution falls. False positives could also increase the 6.2% checkout failure rate if legitimate transactions are blocked, raising the 34 support tickets a day and risking merchant goodwill at a time when 16 of 52 staff still lack advanced cybersecurity training to tune the system. That would weaken the 18,600-transaction quarter and make the $840,000 platform upgrade harder to justify to shareholders.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to ZEN's survey data, failure rate and cost base.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 11.8% rise in cloud hosting costs will affect ZEN. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If the $500,000 five-year loan is variable-rate, the added annual cost is 0.75% × $500,000 = $3,750 a year, which is small beside $264,000 of fixed costs and could be removed by fixing the rate. The indirect effect matters more: dearer credit raises the opportunity cost of the $340,000 retained profit and makes future borrowing for the $840,000 platform less attractive.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, from $12.80 to $13.62): Every paid hour now costs $0.82 more (6.4% × $12.80). The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so no honest annual wage total can be invented; what can be judged is that with 52 staff, labour is a real cost, and the 16 of 52 employees still needing cybersecurity training will be paid at the higher rate while the 6.2% checkout failure rate is being tackled. Unless productivity rises, unit labour cost climbs and the $7.50 contribution is squeezed.

Cloud hosting and data-centre costs (up 11.8%): ZEN runs contactless terminals and online checkout, so hosting is an unavoidable operating input, and 11.8% is a far larger shock than the 0.75-point rate move or the 6.4% wage rise. The insert gives no separate energy or hosting bill, so only the scale and direction can be stated: it lands on every transaction at a time when volumes grew only 5.2%, and it multiplies the cost of the AI screening in the $840,000 upgrade.

Conclusion: The 11.8% rise in cloud hosting costs will have the greatest impact. It is the largest percentage change, it touches every one of the 84,000 units and the 18,600 quarterly transactions rather than one loan or one wage grade, and it cannot be passed on when payment volumes grew only 5.2%. The wage rise is second because it recurs across all 52 staff, while the interest rise is smallest and can be neutralised by fixing the loan rate.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to ZEN.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on ZEN's costs, finance or prices in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that cloud hosting costs have the greatest impact and clear reasons why the other two are smaller.
